text: p.452) and short-term outcomes may also be im- proved in non-diabetics with hyperglycaemia treated with insulin.53 Other early treatments that are being investigated54 in- clude hypothermia, hyperbaric oxygen, calcium modula- tion, and complement inhibitors such as pexelizumab. Early use of stem cell infusions55 or colony-stimulating factors56 to promote myocardial repair has also been tried, but the optimum approach remains unclear.57 Long-term management. Patients who survive the im- mediate post-infarction period remain at high risk for car- diovascular mortality. The main predictors of poor out- come are the extent of left ventricular dysfunction, residual myocardial ischaemia, and ventricular arrhythmias. Fol- low-up should include cardiac rehabilitation and the iden- tification and modification of risk factors for ischaemic heart disease (see Cardiovascular Risk Reduction, p.1164). Exercise testing, echocardiography, myocardial imaging techniques, and pharmacological stress testing (see Myocardial Imaging under Dipyridamole, p.1268) can be used after myocardial infarction to help identify those at high risk for recurrent ischaemic events and to se- lect patients needing coronary angiography.3,4 In patients who develop angina soon after myocardial infarction, ex- ercise testing may be unhelpful and potentially hazardous, although many will need angiography to determine wheth- er angioplasty or bypass surgery is required. Drug therapy is important in the long-term management of patients after myocardial infarction, both for symptom control and for secondary prevention.3,4,58,59 • Aspirin, given during the acute phase and then contin- ued for one to two years, has been shown to reduce mor- tality and re-infarction rates. A meta-analysis60 con- firmed the benefit of prolonged antiplatelet treatment in the secondary prevention of myocardial infarction and patients should receive antiplatelet therapy indefinitely. Clopidogrel appears to be as effective as aspirin61 and should be considered in patients intolerant of, or with contra-indications to, aspirin.
